scenes.text: It's nine p.m. You're out for dinner. Three decisions are waiting on you: a refund, a vendor invoice, a calendar clash. Your team is stuck until you find a laptop.
Greenlight is an approval terminal for Even G2. One request at a time, checked against your own rules, answered with one gesture.

Requests arrive from Telegram, Gmail and Google Calendar. Policy Guard reads the amount first, with plain code, then asks a model to judge it against rules you wrote in English. If the model is down, the card still appears, flagged, with a fallback tag. The AI only recommends. Only your gesture sends anything.
Setup takes a minute. Connect your accounts. Write two or three rules, the way you would brief an assistant. Then pair your glasses with a six-digit code that works once and expires in ten minutes.

Rohan asks for a three-twenty-dollar AWS refund in Telegram. One card: what, who, and a one-line recommendation. Tap to approve. You get three seconds to undo, and then the reply lands right under his message.
A nine-hundred-dollar invoice arrives by email. It breaks your five-hundred-dollar rule, so the card is flagged. Hold to decline, and a polite reply goes back on the same thread.
A new invite overlaps your investor call. Flagged against your no-double-booking rule. Decline it, and the calendar updates.
Every decision is logged: who asked, the verdict, what you chose, and whether the model or the fallback judged it. This is the real dashboard, running locally.
Three promises. Nothing is sent until the countdown ends. A double tap never sends twice. And Greenlight never moves funds. Demo accounts only.
Built during the hackathon: more than eighty commits, a hundred and eighty-eight tests, three channels, one glasses app. The code, the tests and the dashboard are all in the repository.
Greenlight. Read the request. Trust your rules. Decide in one tap.
